analysis.one_liner: Bans state and local governments from offering their own public broadband internet service.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee and never received a vote in the House.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred states, cities, and counties from selling broadband internet to the public, whether retail or wholesale. It contained narrow carve-outs: cities already running networks could keep them only if no more than one commercial competitor served the area, and the Tennessee Valley Authority was exempt. It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Private commercial internet providers, especially cable and phone companies that would otherwise face a publicly owned competitor in areas they serve or have declined to serve.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would prohibit any state or local government from providing or selling retail or wholesale broadband internet access service to the public or to telecommunications providers [S3].
Private providers would no longer face competition from city- or county-owned networks, preserving their existing subscriber bases and pricing in areas they serve [S3].
The bill would bar the Federal Communications Commission from preempting state laws to allow municipal broadband, closing off a route communities had used to expand access [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Residents of areas with slow, expensive, or unavailable private broadband would lose the option of a city-built network. Cities and electric utilities that want to deploy broadband would bear the cost of being barred from doing so.

drawbacks.text: The bill's grandfather clause allows a city network to continue only if the FCC finds no more than one commercial provider competes in the area, so a second private entrant could force shutdown of an existing public network that residents already rely on [S3].

Restricting municipal networks would leave many rural and low-income areas dependent on private providers' investment decisions, which in the many places commercial firms have not built out, could mean continued unavailability or higher prices [S3].

Supporters of the bill would argue government-owned networks unfairly compete with private investment using tax-funded resources; the bill attempts to address this by limiting expansion beyond a city's existing service footprint and by protecting 9-1-1 emergency communications [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits would flow to commercial providers while its costs fall on residents of places private firms have not adequately served. The carve-out for the Tennessee Valley Authority and for 9-1-1 services acknowledges public networks can serve legitimate purposes but leaves most communities without a fallback.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Communications and Technology Subcommittee in February 2021 and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Billy Long introduced the bill on February 18, 2021 [S1].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S5].
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Communications and Technology, where it stayed for the remainder of the 117th Congress [S5].
The bill never advanced past committee and received no vote in either chamber [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cities and counties retained their existing authority to build public broadband networks where state law permits, and residents of areas with public networks kept that option; commercial providers gained nothing because the bill never became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Cities that kept their broadband authority

for.name: Rep. Billy Long
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill prohibiting state and local governments from offering broadband service.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without a hearing, markup, or vote for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Republicans; no Democrats sponsored or cosponsored, and no roll-call votes were ever taken, so the partisan split beyond that is not established.

industries.industry: Commercial broadband providers (cable, telephone, and wireless ISPs)
industries.note: The bill would make private commercial firms the only permitted sellers of broadband to the public, preserving their markets from city-owned competition. For residents in areas these firms have not built out or charge heavily in, the industry's interest in this bill runs against theirs.

industries.industry: Municipal and publicly owned broadband networks
industries.note: Cities, counties, and their electric utilities would be barred from selling broadband, and existing networks could be forced to shut down once a second commercial competitor enters. Public networks are typically built where residents lack affordable service.
The bill explicitly exempts the TVA from the prohibition, letting this federally owned utility continue offering broadband while other public providers are barred.
